utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We understand there are one or two matters to be raised before the witness comes in. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The only matter which we would like to bring to your attention at this stage is not one for which we seek any order or instructions, but simply one we would wish to bring to the attention of the Chamber at this stage. We've indicated already in the past that we were encountering some difficulties with our translations and we wish to indicate first that those are difficulties that are due to the lack of staff and resources with CLSS and not with any sort of unwillingness on their part to assist. But we've been notified that a number of documents which had submitted to CLSS could not be provided to us with the deadline that we had set or with the deadline that would be necessarily meaningful for our purposes. We believe that there approximately 20 documents which appear on our Rule 65 ter list of exhibits which are yet to be fully translated, Your Honour. We also believe that there are between 6 and 8 additional documents for which an application by the Defence to amend its Rule 65 ter list are also still pending. In addition to that, there are a number of documents both Defence exhibits and Prosecution exhibits, for which we have submitted requests for corrections or retranslation of certain terms or phrases. CLSS has also asked us to identify in relation to, I believe, five documents which are multi-pages documents. Those parts which are most relevant to the Defence case and we will try to do that in the coming days having in mind that the entire document may not be available on time for use in the Defence case and even those provisions which we may identify as most relevant to our case may not be brought back to us by CLSS on time, in which case we may have to rely on draft translations. The problems, Your Honour, if any, may arise is twofold as we see it. Expert witness will be coming next week and it may be the case that a couple or a bit more documents may be used with that witness and we would wish, obviously, to have those documents ready for this particular person, for our colleagues from the Prosecution and our ourselves. We will do what we can to obtain those in the form of official translation from CLSS and if not, to try to obtain a draft translation. The other matter and the other reason why we bring that to your attention at this stage, Your Honour, is as indicated there are a number of documents, we believe between ten and fifteen, which may be added to our Rule 65 ter exhibit by way of leave of the Chamber which we would wish to do as soon as possible. At this stage we are waiting for the translation of those documents to be able to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence of Johan Tarculovski is also facing problems in translation. First, I would like to inform the Court that the CLSS has informed us that the translation of the expert report from the military expert for the Defence of Tarculovski, Mr. Blagoja Markovski, will be finished on the 14th of February although it was initially agreed that it would be ready on the 15th of January, and later, the date was prolonged until the 30th of January. This is what the CLSS informed us. Secondly, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the CLSS informed us that the chronology of events of 2001, which is part of the expert report, in accordance with 65 ter 2D685 is refusing to translate in entirety because, according to their rules, this service does not translate documents of this size, only parts or certain paragraphs relevant to us which we would use in this trial. This is why I would ask the Trial Chamber to issue an order for full translation of the chronology of events which are also part of the expert report. At the same time, I would like to inform the Court that, in regards to all other documents, there were no other problems with translation and all others have been translated in time. As for chronology of events of 2001, I would like to inform the Court that this chronology of events was sent for translation on the 29th of December. We were informed that the translation would be finished by the 10th of February. However, in the meantime the CLSS informed us that the documents that the Defence had sent were lost in the system, which, it seems, had happened frequently. This is why the Defence submitted a new request for translation on the 4th of February with a deadline of 18th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski, the chronology, we have not seen it. What period of time does it cover?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This chronology of events covers the time from January 2001 to September 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what events, what is the nature of the events that it covers?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This chronology of events covers incidents that happened and were caused by the terrorist NLA groups in that period, as well as the period of the event which is the case of this trial. It encompasses the activities of the Macedonian security forces in this period of time, which parts of the territory was under the alleged control of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. So it is your submission that all of that chronology is relevant, especially to the issue of whether there is an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And we believe it would be fair also for the Prosecution to have this document in its entirety in order to facilitate a more comprehensive cross-examination of the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how -- how long is this chronology, how big?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 142 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does it record the birthdays of every participant? It does seem a very long chronology. Not having seen it, it's very difficult to make any useful comment, but I'm sure quite a bit of what is in that chronology is going to be relevant to the issues in this case. But I would have thought that 140 pages was probably very much an excessively detailed chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will -- I will promise this Court that part of this chronology, which is perhaps redundant or superfluous will be taken out and thus reduce the number of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that would be a very constructive move, Mr. Apostolski. You will appreciate that we need to know that certain material military type events occurred and some political events; but we don't need a full summary of everything that happened in each military event or in each political event, and there will be some things that occurred that you will see immediately are of virtually no use in the end. If can you look through that carefully and cut down the chronology significantly, I'm sure it will help. The issue is very simple as both you and Mr. Mettraux are aware. Macedonian is not a language which this Tribunal is equipped to deal with fully in either translation or interpretation, and it is therefore difficult to obtain the services of enough people with the required degree of skill and reliability, and that's particularly so in the area of translation; and, therefore, we are simply overtaxing the capacity of the CLSS to deal with what is being put before them by the two Defence teams. We have, in truth, only one person working full time here, and a number of other people working part of their time from outside the Tribunal, trying to help us to get the work done and there's simply too much work to achieve it. So if you can cut down and the same, of course, goes for Mr. Mettraux, and it goes for anything that the Prosecution may be putting before the CLSS. I don't know whether at the moment anything is. But if you can cut it down to what is really important, at least that can then be done as a matter of priority. It may then be possible to have a little more done a little later, but still in time to be used in the case. But if there can be a serious effort made to deal with the work that only is of real important significance to our work, that can be dealt with as a matter of priority and hopefully we'll be able to keep the trial running without delay. Because the other alternative is we simply have to delay until the service can catch up. So thank you for suggesting that you will look at the chronology, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one matter, Your Honour, while we're on the subject of translations. Today, it came to my attention that the Book of Rules of the organisation and work of the Ministry of Interior has been admitted into evidence actually in two different versions. The first time it was admitted as P33 with a partial translation. And subsequently to that, it was tendered by the Defence with a full English translation as Exhibit 1D107. In both cases, Your Honour, we have draft translations from CLSS, and the Prosecution, of course, is extremely grateful for the strenuous efforts that CLSS has made and continues to make to keep up with all of the translation demands. But the Prosecution has noticed that, for example, there are some differences in the two English translations. And because there are many, many documents that have been admitted in this trial and the use of language and meaning of language and even the nuances of language may be quite important at the end of the day, we may, with the agreement of the Defence, send this matter back to CLSS for a final English translation so that when it's time to write the judgment there will be absolutely no confusion as to what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure they'll be delighted to receive it, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that. Any other matter? Well, I think we will now have the witness. While the witness comes could I mention that, once again today we're going to try another slight rearrangement of our sitting hours and we will plan to finish by around 6.30 this evening with sitting hours divided almost equally into three. We'll see how that goes. And probably tomorrow night, tomorrow afternoon, that is, we will do something similar, and we will then assess whether any permanent any change ought to be made or we will revert to what had been our normal pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made still applies, of course. Now, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stojkov. You will remember that when we left off yesterday evening we had just finished looking at a number of files where the working group on war crimes had investigated crimes allegedly committed by ethnic Albanians. And you may recall that in your testimony on Monday you were asked by my learned colleague whether had you any prejudices that influenced your work in the working group, and you described an incident where an Albanian came to you and complained about a theft of tractor batteries and this was investigated and a Macedonian was charged. And for reference this is at transcript page 8890. Do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojkov, do you consider the theft of tractor batteries to be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll allow me to explain. This happened in the village of Aracinovo where some armed activities also took place. This theft was in a warehouse of a person who was forced to leave his home, because this was a place where military activities did take place and this was a substantial case of theft. We felt that this was part of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So just to be perfectly clear, Mr. Stojkov, you're saying that this case of theft was actually a war crime.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the binder with your documents, there was a complaint about a theft of 116.000 Deutschemarks. This is a theft that happened in a place where military activities took place. I mean to say that this theft befallen upon an ethnic Albanian was carried out by persons of ethnic Macedonians who were then in the reserve police forces. As a result, we felt that this is one of the criminal acts committed in a place of military conflict by uniformed and armed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in that case, do you know what was done to the reservists who had committed this theft?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aggrieved party of Albanian ethnicity reported this theft at the police station Petrovac which is under the police station Gazi Baba where I was inspector at that period. After the theft was reported, the inspectors and police officers undertook all necessary measures to find the perpetrators. Among other things, several houses were searched of persons who were suspect of allegedly committed the theft and these items were found. And after the case was documented, it was submitted to the public prosecutor's office, a criminal report was submitted, and these persons were sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And how were these individuals identified?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to operative tactical measures undertaken by inspectors and police officers, information was obtained that they might have been the perpetrators. I think it was three persons in question. I don't know how this information was obtained. Most probably in some of the controls that were carried out, some of the stolen objects were found. After establishing the identity of these persons, additional operative measures were undertaken, including search of houses and other premises, during which part of the stolen goods were found and returned to the aggrieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you know what the outcome of this case was? Do you know whether any -- sorry. Let me rephrase that. Do you know what the outcome of this case was?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the criminal report was forwarded to the public prosecutor's office, it was then in their hand, which was then processed in the form of an indictment to the court. I cannot know whether the court found them guilty or not, whether they're in prison or not, whether there was -- they were remanded in custody or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know whether these individuals were dismissed from the list of reservists for the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these were dismissed or not. I -- according to me, not only should they have been dismissed from the list of reservists but they should be in jail because they committed a criminal act in uniform and with weapons where military activities took place. They abused the trust given to them as members of the reserve police forces. In my opinion, the punishment should be rigorous in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, apart from this case of theft in your time with the working group, how many other allegations of war crimes did you investigate where the perpetrators were members of the Macedonian security forces?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say an exact number, but all of the activities we carried out had, as a starting point, the reports of aggrieved parties which we received most probably from the analytics sectors of the police stations. I recall there were a number of cases of theft, of -- destruction of homes, but I cannot be more precise than this. It was a long time ago. I remember this case because I was working on it myself and so I know a little bit more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, if you can't remember exact numbers of how many you investigated, are you able to remember any specific cases?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please explain and elaborate a little bit further? Cases of Macedonians having committed theft or other crime in this period?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm asking if can you recall any other specific cases of war crimes committed by members of the Macedonian security forces.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely. I remember there was a case of a physical assault by a police reservist in Tetovo, but I cannot elaborate more on this case, because when we visited Tetovo, and in view of the fact that OVR in Tetovo worked only partially and not in a regular fashion, because of the military activities, and we undertook most of the activities they had to carry out. I know a procedure was carried against this one or two police reservists who had physically assaulted persons on some of the check-points in Tetovo, but I cannot tell you precisely. I know I read the material and it's in the case files of the materials that we took but I cannot precisely explain to you how all of this was finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: These cases that you speak of, two or more that involved investigations of Macedonian security force members, would these files have been sent to the analytics department for filing in the same manner as all your other files were?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, all of our activities, for example, if I went to official working visit to police units in Tetovo, or other services in Tetovo, upon my return all the materials which we took back in copies were documented in an Official Note about where we went, who we met, and what documents we took. And in all of these cases, and all of this which I have done and I have told you about should be in the analytics department of the MOI.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. So there was no difference depending on who the alleged perpetrators were in what you did with these files?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the working group, I came in September 2001, when all military activities or when the armed conflict in Macedonia was over; perhaps not fully over, but for the most part, it was. And I said that, for me, there cannot be a difference between a Macedonian Albanian child or a civilian or anyone else from a different ethnicity because this is not only Macedonians or Albanians in question, there was also other mixed populations, Serbs, Romas all ethnic communities living in Macedonia. I'm talking myself personally; I cannot comment about my colleagues or other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I wasn't clear there, Mr. Stojkov. My question was meant to be a little simpler than that and my question was: Did you send all your files to the same place for storage or for filing, regardless of who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All case files, accompanied by Official Note, were sent to the analytics unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So can you think of any reason why no files of investigations into members of the Macedonian security forces would be found in a search of the Ministry of Interior archives where the files you have been shown earlier were located?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain why this is so. If a case was processed, then such documents also exist in the basic public prosecution. In the previous case which I spoke about, there should be documents that a criminal report against these person was filed and that further measures were taken. I don't know why these cases are not to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just to move on to a slightly different topic. Do you recall yesterday I asked you about what would happen if a crime was widely known throughout Macedonia, perhaps through media reports, but no complaints came forward and you stated and I quote: "I think if there had been such an event in my country, in the Republic of Macedonia, certainly a way would have been found to investigate the case, to arrive at the basic data, what had happened, and what needs to be undertaken. However, I don't think anything of the sort had happened thus far without it being detected." This is at transcript page 8955. Do you recall saying that, Mr. Stojkov?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn to tab 12 in your binder, please. And this is Exhibit P00324. Do you have a document in front of you from Human Rights Watch entitled: Letter to Macedonian prime minister Ljubco Georgievski?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you see the date, May 4, 2001?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you see in the second paragraph it states: "Reports of the renewed conflict in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia between security forces and armed groups of ethnic Albanians raise concerns relating to adherence to international humanitarian law." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if you down two paragraphs from there, Mr. Stojkov, I will read what this paragraph states: "This concern is strengthed by our findings following the March 2001 actions by its security forces against armed ethnic Albanian groups in the western part of the country. Available sources suggest that government forces were responsible for the deliberate killing of 16-year-old Omer Shabani on April 3 in the village of Selce. We also received reports that families of ethnic Albanians arrested on suspicion of membership in the so-called National Liberation Army were unable to obtain any information on the whereabouts of the -- finally of --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: "Finally our documentation suggests that government forces were responsible for the wanton destruction and looting of villages perceived as being pro-NLA, including the villages of Selce, Gjermo, Gajre, Drenovec, and Kolte. We urge you to make these incidents the subject of prompt, thorough and transparent investigations." Did you follow that, Mr. Stojkov?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you aware if your working group investigated the allegations regarding the killing of Omer Shabani in Selce?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is a document that I see for the first time now. This is a document I was not aware of. And secondly, if it was reported to the police stations or to the OVR, it should have been Tetovo, or I think that these villages gravitate to Tetovo. If we had received it among the documents, within the overview of the other cases, then I suppose we had processed it. If we had not received it then we had not processed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you specifically recall having done an investigation into this case?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any allegations of wanton destruction and looting by the Macedonian security forces in these villages?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the conflict period, as far as I see it, this is an event of March 2001. I don't know where these villages are but I know that they are in the vicinity of Tetovo some where. I know that during that time the Albanian terrorists were in the vicinity of Tetovo, the UCK, the NLA, so I don't know whether the Macedonian police entered these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: My question was something different. My question was: Were you aware of allegations of wanton destruction and looting by the Macedonian security forces?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that, to the best of your knowledge, there was no investigation into these allegations?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I see that my colleague is standing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object because I believe that this question is unfounded. The witness answered the question before that. He was not aware of the event so there is no basis to ask him whether he is aware of any investigation that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can get an answer to the question, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, I'll repeat the question. Would it be fair to say that, to the best of your knowledge, there was no investigation into these allegations?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, that, first of all, I was not aware of those events. And, secondly, I could not know whether there had been an investigation. So the answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, thank you. If you can now turn to tab 14. This is another document from Human Rights Watch. It's dated August 22, 2001. And the heading is: "Police abuse against Albanians continues in Macedonia. Peace agreement doesn't end violence." And if you can go down, it's should be the second-to-last paragraph, starting: "On Monday, August 13, 2001 ..." Do you see that? This should be in the second-to-last paragraph, Mr. Stojkov, I believe. Perhaps if you look at the document on the screen in front of you, Mr. Stojkov, I can see it there, the second-to-last paragraph that appears on the screen in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. Yes, I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this states: "On Monday, August 13, 2001, police officers guarding Skopje's main hospital arrested four ethnic Albanians who had come to the hospital to pick up an elderly Albanian relative undergoing kidney dialysis treatment. The police searched their car and claimed to find a bullet in the trunk. The police then proceeded to beat the four men in the street." It continues: "The men were then taken on to the hospital grounds and beaten continuously for several hours with heavy metal cables, baseball bats, police truncheons, and gun butts amidst cheering from the civilian crowd that had gathered. Following this, the four men were taken to the Beko 1 police station where they were subjected to more beatings, had urine and burning cigarettes thrown at them, and were threatened with execution. Following interventions from their ethnic Macedonian lawyer and a police officer who knew the men, they were released the next morning. One of the men, 29-year-old Nazmi Aliu, father of a six-year-old and two-year-old, died that day at the hospital from the injuries he received from the police beatings." Now this was in August -- on August 13th, 2001. Were you aware of this incident, Mr. Stojkov?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not informed of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So this incident happened on the streets of Skopje involving police apparently with civilians watching and you're saying that this never came to your notice or attention?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw from the text that an attorney was involved, so since an attorney was involved, if he had been an attorney, he would have reported the case to the competent services and that case would have reached our working group. Most probably the case was not reported and I had not received it in my overview and this is why I am not aware of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You didn't read about this case at all in the newspapers at the time?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in August. At that time I was still performing other tasks. I was still not a member of the working group; I was performing other tasks, and this is the first time that I hear about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to move on now specifically into your working group's investigation into the events in Ljuboten. And you will recall that you testified that Apostol Stojanovski asked to you open a file about the events in Ljuboten. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you recall saying that you questioned that decision, as you said there had been no complaint, and he told you that this was a task given by your superiors. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reacted and we received this task from our coordinator of our working group, Apostol Stojanovski, who had a contact with our superior officers because I had not received in the overview of injured parties and of events the Ljuboten event was not included. I was only working on the basis of overview that I received from the police stations, on the basis of the cases that were reported and events reported, and this is why I reacted in this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, the question I have is when he told you that this was a task given by your superiors, do you know who these superiors were?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time, superior officers or senior officers in the Ministry of the Interior who were able to give orders through Mr. Apostol Stojanovski were the under-secretary, Mr. Spasen Sofevski, the director of BJB, a public security bureau, Mr. Goran Mitevski.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So, would it be fair to say, Mr. Stojkov, that senior officers in the Ministry of Interior had some authority over operative work?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative work is performed by operatives, that is inspectors, of any rank. Our superior officers, I can't really interpret the law what are their obligations or what are their competences but I can't say one way or another whether they could be operatives in the field or are they senior officers with other competences. I can't tell you that. I was an operative and I worked in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, to your knowledge, and I'll leave this to you to answer, obviously, but are you aware whether Ljube Boskoski had anything to do with the decision to investigate this case?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, I'm saying again, I don't remember the exact date. The coordinator, Mr. Apostol Stojanovski came and during a working meeting he explained that the senior officers, he did not mention any names so I don't know who they were, gave us the task to open Ljuboten case file and to start the standard procedures when opening a case file. I don't know whether the then minister, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, was the initiator for the work of that working group or whether he was interested or whether it was Mr. Goran Mitevski or whether it was someone else. I had no way of knowing that myself, since the difference there ranks was such that I was inspector and the gentleman was a minister so I had no direct contact with him, not once during my work in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Isn't that correct that the order to perform this investigation into the events in Ljuboten came from higher up in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is leading the witness because -- in the wrong way. I don't think the witness ever said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not my understanding. Carry on, please, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So to repeat my question, Mr. Stojkov, isn't that correct that the order to perform this investigation came from higher up in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who gave that order to Mr. Apostol Stojanovski, I don't know. But surely that is someone with a higher rank than him, within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stojkov, could you please turn to tab 19 in your binder. And this is Exhibit P00073. And do you see the heading: Decision to establish a commission, and it's dated 13.8.2001. Do you see that? And if I read the first paragraph it states --

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. It states: "Decision to establish a commission, a commission is established to consider the circumstances and analyse the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to repel the armed attacks by terrorist groups on 12.8.2001 in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje." Do you follow that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you see at the bottom that it has the name of the minister of internal affairs, Ljube Boskoski. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now at the time that your working group started its investigation into the Ljuboten events, were you aware that Minister Boskoski had already set up a commission to investigate the same events?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document is something that I see now for the first time. I don't know whether there was another committee dealing with this. This is what I see for the first time now. I was not informed, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any other bodies within the Ministry of Interior that were also investigating the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, and I know that the analytics department was working on some information, more comprehensive information around the Ljuboten events. This is what I know. With more detailed information. I know that in one of the meetings Mrs. Sofija Galeva - this is when I met her for the first time - was also interested in part of the work of our working group, possibly the Ljuboten event as well. I can't remember. Those are the things that I encountered during my work. This committee and this document are something that I'm just becoming aware now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know who in the analytics department was working on a similar investigation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. My contacts with the analytics department were limited to several meetings with Mrs. Katica Jovanovska when I was bringing some materials to her; otherwise, I don't know who are the other people in the analytics department. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can I just clarify what you meant by stating that "you know that someone -- that the analytics department was working on some information, more comprehensive information, around the Ljuboten events," are you saying that the information that these people had was more comprehensive than what you had?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that our documents, I told you that Mrs. Katica Jovanovska was preparing a broader information regarding the event. Since our documents maybe went -- probably went to her because she was in the analytics department. I don't know -- I don't understand your question. What other -- I know that it was Mrs. Katica Jovanovska from the analytics department. I don't even know the other individuals there because she was the only one that I had contacts with on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, what I'm interested in is what exactly you meant by the phrase "more comprehensive information around the Ljuboten events." What did you mean by "more comprehensive information"?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analytics department receives all materials related to all events on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. The analytics department of the ministry has access to all and any information, documents. I wanted to say that the information that they have, they don't have the duty to communicate those to us. We forward all information that we have to them. They might have had more information than us because all the other services that were working in the field, police stations, the OVRs, had the task to forward all documents and information to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, did you ask the analytics department for access to the documents that they did have?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are failing to understand the competences. We don't have the competence unless a superior officer further up in the hierarchy allows it. We do not have the competence to request any document if this is not ordered or allowed by a superior officer. We did not ask for any documents or at least I personally did not request any documents from the analytics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, don't you think that any additional documents would have helped you in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe now from -- in hindsight, yes. But then I did not think so, and I -- or I had no opportunity to request such documents. I can't really say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that you -- you didn't approach any of your superiors to request access to these documents?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not request any of my superiors to grant me access to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this. I don't know. I simply didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, can you turn to tab 20 next, please. And this is Exhibit P00378. And you'll see, Mr. Stojkov, that this the report of the commission that Minister Boskoski had established on 13 August 2001. And this report is dated 4 September 2001. And the subject of this report, you'll see this in the first paragraph is: "An examination of the circumstances and an analysis of the activities undertaken by the security forces for the Ministry of Interior to repulse armed attacks by terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So would you agree that this commission was investigating much the same events as your working group was?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree, but I am seeing this document for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If you could go to the bottom of page 5. This is on page 5. It's the bottom of page 4 in the English version. And you'll see a heading: "Opinion." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this states: "The activities which were carried out by the security forces of the Ministry of the Interior to repulse the armed attacks of the terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten, Skopje, were well-founded, justified, and properly undertaken yet there is evidently a slight tolerable degree of individual overstepping of the boundaries of the prescribed powers carried out by a small number of members of the Ministry of the Interior who actively participated in the event." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you reach a similar conclusion from your analysis of the documents you had?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the working group, I can say that our working group was disbanded earlier, and there were many case files which I had not finished. If I had finished them, perhaps I would have been able to say whether I agree or not. At this moment, I cannot comment what I'm seeing now, because I'm seeing it for the first time, and I cannot give my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm not asking for your opinion on what this report says so much as to whether you came to the conclusion that this report states in the course of your investigation. Is that what you found in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that my investigation was cut short. I had not finished it, and therefore I'm not able to give you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to the -- the last page of the document, please. And there you will see a list, not so much a list but you'll see three names at the bottom of the document. And the first name you'll see is Goran Mitevski. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you've testified that you met with Goran Mitevski on a number of occasions in the course of your work with the working group, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you discussed the progress of your investigation into the Ljuboten case?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we talked about the work on all cases and case files that the working group was charged with. If we talked about all, this means that we were also discussing the Ljuboten case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mitevski ever mention to you that he had been part of a commission that had performed its own investigation into the case?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anything to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mitevski ever offer you access to documents that he had, or that this working group, this commission had put together in its investigation into Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a director in the ministry, Mr. Goran Mitevski received information from us. He was not obliged to give us feedback information. Therefore, I have not received information or documents about a particular case from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, did you ever request the assistance of the UBK sector of the MOI to identify any useful information relating to the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, as a working group, our competencies are not such that we can request any information from the UBK. They can use our information; we could not request information from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you speak to a superior, someone higher up the command in the Ministry of Interior, to see if you could gain access to any information that the UBK might have?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not speak myself. Maybe the coordinator did, but whether this was approved or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just to move on to the next point. You've testified that in the course of your investigation what you did do was to visit the Mirkovci and Cair police stations, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I waited for my learned colleague to finish what he was saying but I'd just like to mention that on page 25, line 5 instead of the words recorded "evidentirano" the word obvious or "ocigledno" was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Evidently was used. The word evidently used instead of -- recorded "evidentirano."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, do you recall testifying about speaking with the deputy commander of Mirkovci police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you recall saying that he told you that people and some weapons had been brought into Mirkovci police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you ask for the names of the people who had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All persons that are brought in the police station have to be recorded in the daily log-book but we were not interested in this. We were interested in written documents in the form of a note, written information whether this -- the process of recording was done in the proper fashion to make a copy of it and to take it with us, which we did later in the police station Cair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And the documents you recovered from police station Cair, did they have the names of the people who had been brought in to Mirkovci police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a document with the persons that were brought in from the police station Mirkovci, and I think that we took a copy of this document with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you ask the deputy commander of Mirkovci police station for the names of the police officers who had brought these individuals into the station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy commander of the police station said that on the day of the event he was not in the police station. He was out. However, I told you that in -- that our discussions with this persons are on a voluntary basis. Each if we had spoken with some of the police officers, we could not have made this an official document because these persons did not want to give an official statement or an Official Note to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, you actually testified several occasions about people in Mirkovci police station and Cair police station who did not want to speak to you. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were police officers in the police station Mirkovci. I remember when we went in the duty officer in police station Mirkovci was not of Macedonian ethnicity. We introduced ourselves. He introduced himself, but I cannot remember the name. I know there were additionally several police officers in the hallway of the police station. I can describe to you this police station and the premises. In our discussions with them in the hallway, I know that one of them introduced himself as Dragan and told him that on that day he was at work and that he submitted a lot of Official Notes which are in the analytics in the police station Cair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: That wasn't the specific question I asked you, Mr. Stojkov. The question I asked is: Do you recall testifying that there were people in the Mirkovci police station who did not want to speak to you, at least formally?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I said that in the police station Mirkovci there were police officers, not people, who did not formally want to give statements regarding the events of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So did you speak to Apostol Stojanovski or any of your superiors about their reluctance to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this on the working meeting but we cannot force anyone to give an official statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you seek an order from any of your superiors for these people to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we held these people as suspects, or rather, if they were suspects, if someone had reported that these people had committed a crime that we would have reported this to our superiors or with the internal control which would undertaken the remaining measures. And these people, if there was grounds or it was proven that they had committed a crime, then we would have submitted a report to that extent, because there was no report against these people. We had no basis or ground to make these people or police officers give any statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an error in the transcript. It is on page 30, line 3, what was recorded was that the witness said these people were suspects; whereas the witness in fact said had these people been suspects or if those people had been suspects and then he carried on with what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just to follow on that from that, Mr. Stojkov. If I could hear it from you yourself again, were you saying that these people were suspects or in fact did you say had they been suspects?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was clear. If a person, even police officers, were suspects, then we would have undertaken the remaining measures. We would have informed the internal control or superiors about undertaking further measure to prove whether they committed a crime or not. Because these persons were not suspect under any basis or any grounds, we could not force them to give official statements about this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Regardless of forcing them to give official statements, did you at least seek some assistance from your superiors to perhaps encourage them to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no grounds to ask such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, you were investigating the events in Ljuboten, weren't you, and these people may well have had useful information. Wouldn't you say that was grounds?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: My grounds would be that I would unjustifiably accuse them of having committed a crime. I did not therefore have grounds. How could I ask of bodies up in the hierarchy to be examined officially? That means that he is accused or a witness to a certain event. If this was so, then this would have been processed by the public prosecutor's office or the courts and then he would be called in as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So are you saying from that that just speaking to someone effectively means that person is a suspect?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I spoke with these persons and that there is no official material about what I spoke to them about. If there is no such official material, that means it is as if I did not speak to them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So if it's as if you did not speak to them at all, you effectively haven't gained any information from these people that might help your investigation, have you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I establish contact with the police officers in police stations Mirkovci and Cair. I had unofficial conversations with my colleagues because they did not want to speak officially. The information which they told me was used as much as we could as members of the working group. But since there is no official document of this, I could not have processed these materials and used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: To move on, Mr. Stojkov, yesterday my colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, before you move on, this may be a convenient time, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, you will recall that yesterday when we looked through some of the files of your working group, we saw that in several of them there were medical records and you testified that in these cases the injured persons or their family members had provided those records. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And regardless of who provided these medical records, would it be fair to say that obviously they were considered to be useful in the investigations that you performed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could be useful if used to prepare a criminal report, or if they are forwarded to the public prosecutor's office so that they draft the indictment on the basis of that. But for me, as a police officer, other than collecting and gathering them, I do not understand them, because those are medical documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday that you did not seek the medical records for Atulla Qaili because it wasn't your job to collect medical information from the hospital. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task was not to collect medical files from the hospitals because I told you that the injured parties brought them while in the case of the deceased person, because the case was taken from the basic public prosecutor's office and the investigating judge was informed about the case; that is, according to the documents, the official documents that I had seen at that time, all future actions that we would have taken would have been taken upon request from the public prosecutor or the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, you did perform some actions to investigate that didn't come on request from the public prosecutor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We undertook measures that we are able to undertake as authorised officers of the Ministry of the Interior. Until the moment when a case is forwarded to the basic public prosecutor's office or to the investigating judge, until then, we take the measures that we are authorised to take under the law. At a moment when the case goes into the hands of the basic public prosecutor or the investigating judge, then we only take measures upon their request.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you point to any specific rules or regulations that prevented you from seeking these medical records?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not a lawyer, so I cannot explain specific laws. However, we were not prevented from seeking them. Those were not our tasks, simply. If we went to take them, I'm certain the hospitals or the medical institutions would have looked for some authorisation to do that because we were not authorised at that time to get the medical documents. If I would go there and introduce myself, I'm a police officer, I need the medical files on that person, I don't think there is such methodology in our work. There is a process on how you obtain the medical files related to a case. It is either the hospital or the medical institution that forwards them to the police institutions or the injured parties, after they leave the hospital or their relatives when reporting the case, bring the files with them and give them to the competent police bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you have spoken to a doctor to ask about what happened to Atulla Qaili?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally would have been able to talk to a doctor, but that would go beyond my competences because that would have meant a private investigation. In the case of the person, Atulla Qaili, the public prosecutor's office and the investigating judge were already informed. That would mean me circumventing their powers or abusing my powers. I could not take measures without their knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did the public prosecutor or the investigating judge have knowledge that you were performing the investigation that you were performing?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, whether they knew that we were operating as a working group or not. I know that we had a contact with the public prosecutor's office, with the public prosecutor of the time, in terms that we were collecting evidence on potential war crimes committed at the territory of Macedonia. And I had two meetings with the gentleman from the public prosecutor's office, I believe I said that. So if I had meetings with them they should have been aware, it seems, that we existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did the public prosecutor or investigating judge direct to you go to OVR Cair to collect documentation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. My coordinator sent me there when he received an order from some superior officer. Whether it was the prosecutor's office or the court that requested that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So when you went to OVR Cair to collect these documents, you didn't have knowledge of any official authorisation from the public prosecutor or the judge, did you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware. Actually, I can't understand the question. We went to document and to find all written documents related to the events in the period related to Ljuboten event. Who authorised this and how, I don't know. I was given the task by my coordinator who had received the task from one of the senior officers and we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Stojkov, you also stated that another reason that you didn't seek out the medical records in relation to Atulla Qaili was because you were not authorised to investigate the cause of death of any individual. This is at transcript page 8930. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As an inspector, I am not a homicide inspector. I remember that statement. I was authorised only to collect the documents and documentary evidence, written materials that indicated or were related to some events. And we needed to open a case file to gather evidence and then we forwarded that to the competent bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, wasn't a major part of the Ljuboten case that you were investigating finding out how certain villagers in Ljuboten had died?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specifically saw in the materials until the exhumation. And unfortunately, we were not allowed to be present at the exhumation and we expected to receive the materials from the exhumation but we did not receive them. From the materials that I saw at this Cair police station, when reading the materials, I learned that one person had died only at the city hospital in Skopje and that person was previously taken by a medical team from the Mirkovci police station. So I was aware only of that case, that one person had died. I was not aware of other cases of deceased persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Didn't you say earlier on in your testimony upon questioning by my colleague Ms. Residovic that when you had spoken to Mr. Krstevski at Cair police station he had mentioned that he had information that people had died in the village. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were persons killed, not dead, in the village. So we're speaking about a difference here, because we are speaking about persons killed in the village that were later buried without the presence and without an investigation, while a deceased person is a person who died at the city hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojkov, I'm a little confused and perhaps you can clear this up for me. What exactly were you investigating about Ljuboten? What events were you investigating?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task was to go obtain and file all documents and data related to the Ljuboten event. What exactly happened on that day. Whether there were persons brought the in. What happened to the persons who were brought in. Where were those persons taken and what were their data. We asked whether there were reports coming from injured parties, aggrieved persons, whether they were injured or whether someone was beaten or in other way physically ill-treated. However, at the police station there were no reports, no complainants, persons or their families that some people have been injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So you're saying that the dead individuals in Ljuboten, that was not part of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when we were reading the documents, apart from the data received from a person from the village that there were bodies of killed persons in the village and that those persons were later buried, certainly on the village cemetery, apart from that data, and the data on the person who had died in the -- at the hospital, we had no other data about what precisely happened to those persons. Our objective was, if possible, to establish contacts with some of the individuals from the village, because, as far as we understood from our conversations, the colleagues made attempts, they had initial data but later they were refused because the population from the village refused to cooperate with the police. It was agreed during one of our meetings that we try again to establish contact with any person from the village who would be able to give us more precise data regarding the events and the murder or the death of those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Killing, instead of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And when you testified about the efforts that were made to contact villagers in Ljuboten, you said that Ljube Krstevski told you that no one from Ljuboten was willing to speak to the police. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the chief said that the local population from the Ljuboten village did not want to cooperate and have contacts or interviews with the police bodies. In one of the materials that we later saw at the police station, I found out that they made efforts, they made attempts to establish contacts with some of the people from Ljuboten to learn about the bodies that were there, the bodies of persons killed or dead. However, they failed at that. There were some contacts. The contacts were terminated, and later there was no contact between the police and the population of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And didn't you testify that in fact you made contact yourself with some villagers?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know several individuals who still live presently in the village of Ljuboten. I personally attempted and established some contacts with those individuals but I could not receive more specific data because it was still the post-conflict period and the persons refused to discuss that case. Since the contact was established following a line of private friendships, those persons did not want to give official statement, although I could have used those unofficial information, I would have relayed those information to my superior officers and I would have taken further measure. But I'm saying again, I am still in contact with those friends of mine who live in Ljuboten village and they refused to discuss anything that happened there. The post-conflict period was still on in our Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What were the names of these individuals that you contacted?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I got a message from one of my friends who still live at Ljuboten village last night, but I certainly can't divulge their names here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And wouldn't you agree, Mr. Stojkov, that because you weren't able to speak to any villagers from Ljuboten you really weren't able to get a full picture of the events that happened in that village?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: But wouldn't you also agree that there were other sources out there besides the villagers that you could have used to build up a better picture of what occurred?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't understand what you're saying. The only source that we were able to use at the moment, pursuant to our operational procedures was the police station. This is where we started and this is where we obtained the initial information and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you aware that an organisation called Human Rights Watch performed an investigation into the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of that organisation, but during that period in Macedonia there were several non-governmental international other organisations, Red Cross and I don't know what else. I don't know what they did and what were they working on. That was not my task to contact them, nor, if they requested, through the police bodies, some information, I'm sure they were given that information, but I was not able and I had no contacts with them so that I could ask for any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you please turn to tab 22, Mr. Stojkov. This is Exhibit P00352. And it's a Human Rights Watch report. And if you could turn to the second page. This is the page with the ERN U000-0099. Do you see a page with a heading: "Crimes against civilians, abuses by Macedonian forces in Ljuboten, August 10 to 12, 2001." This should be the second page in the Macedonian copy that you have, Mr. Stojkov. It's the page which is on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you see from that, Mr. Stojkov, that Human Rights Watch conducted an investigation into the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page U000-0103. And this should be -- in the English version it's the eighth page, it has page number six at the bottom. And if we could go to the bottom of the page. I believe that -- could we go one page further in the Macedonian version. Thank you. If you look at the bottom of the page there, Mr. Stojkov, you see a number of footnotes. Do you see what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can you see that these refer to a number of interviews with individuals from Ljuboten village. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And it provides their names?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you agree it might have been useful to contact Human Rights Watch to perhaps get their assistance in seeking the cooperation of the Ljuboten villagers?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. However, this cooperation could not be established by me without informing my superiors of this or without having this come as a proposal from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you suggest it to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not propose this because, at this time, I did not know that Human Rights Watch were carrying out their own investigation about the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Were you aware that the OSCE had conducted an investigation into the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the OSCE was there on the day of the events and afterwards. This is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So was any attempt made by your working group to contact the OSCE for their assistance in establishing contact with the villagers in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you contact any ethnic Albanian politicians or community leaders to seek their help in getting the cooperation of the villagers?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Why was none of this done?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I'm employed and a member of the MOI. My work procedure is strictly regulated. I'm an employee of the MOI of the Republic of Macedonia. All materials and evidence is received by the ministry, not by other unofficial sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: But would you agree that this -- information perhaps that these organisations may have been able to provide or assistance they may have been able to give would have been useful in your investigation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. If I had part of those information at the time, I surely would have used it, if they had been submitted to the ministry, or if I had them in the case that they had been submitted to the ministry as official documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if your work procedure was strictly regulated and you could only perform tasks according to those regulations, then why did you go and speak to friends from the village?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I was in the village but that I contacted my friends who live in the village. This is the first thing. Second, I told you how the procedure went. Report by the injured party or members of family in the police station, and an overview which I received, I don't know who prepared this overview, the analytics department or someone else. This is how we received the basic information and this is -- was the starting point for my work onwards. I established contacts from my friends from the village of Ljuboten because I wanted to obtain information that could be helpful in my further work. If the friends I had there pointed to a party that had been injured and said that they -- that he or she wanted to talk to me and wanted to submit an official report about any kind of injury, then I would continue much better and much more effectively to carry out my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, yesterday and the day before you were shown a number of documents by my colleague Ms. Residovic that came from OVR Cair, and you were asked several times whether these documents confirmed the information that you had. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which documents you were referring to. If the transcript so states, then so it is. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So you do remember being shown documents and agreeing that these corroborated the information that you had?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown documents that were brought by the analytics department at the police station Cair. From most of them, I had information and I know what those -- what that information contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Basically, if I could sum up perhaps my understanding of what you've said and what this means, is that the documents that you were shown that were prepared by police officers from those police stations corroborated what police officers from those same stations had told you in person. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these documents were prepared by the police officers who were working there when I was there - some of them told me that they had been working there - but some of these documents were prepared by authorised police officers who were on duty that day in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And these documents prepared by whichever police officers simply corroborated what you had been told informally by other police officers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents corroborate only the things which happened those days. By description and in text, the events before, during and after were depicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that informally off the record some officers at police station had told you that the people who had been brought to Cair had been injured not by police officers but by Macedonian villagers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just that -- it's not just that they told me but there were also documents which show that, at one point of time, population of Macedonian ethnicity entered in a situation of conflict between the Macedonians and Albanians, during which the police officers succeeded in extracting the Albanians from the conflict with the Macedonians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, let me read to you a section from the transcript and this is at page 8906 and we'll see if you recall this. The question was asked: "Mr. Stojkov, you have just related to us the story of Mr. Krstevski and a number of your colleagues about people attacking villagers and the police trying to save them. Did you find all that plausible, the stories that your colleagues shared with you?" And you answered: "Of course I did believe the stories primarily because they are my colleagues. They are authorised officers and, pursuant to the law, they need to safeguard the law and order." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember and then I went on to say that I had the opportunity to see with my own eyes when I was going home on that day, to see lots of people, Macedonian citizens, citizens of Macedonian ethnicity who were in front of the police station and up in the village and settlement of Radisani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, can I take it from your statement that: "I did believe the stories primarily because they are my colleagues," that over your long time in the police force you've come to trust and accept the words of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I would not qualify them as stories because these are not stories; these are events. When joining the ministry, each person knows the legal obligations and the tasks he or she is charged with. In addition to the rules of the ministry, there are also moral rules that a police officer must fulfil, and I trust my colleagues and what they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: All right. So after being told by your colleagues that these villagers from Ljuboten have been injured by Macedonian villagers, would be it be fair to say you're inclined to accept that because you trust the word of policemen, of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events, which I later heard from my colleagues, I was also able to read in documents from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And these documents were prepared by policemen, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a police station, they are prepared by police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you found what they had to say plausible, and you accepted that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
