utterances.text: I accepted this because in the police station Cair and Mirkovci, there was no record of anyone having been reported as an injured person. If there had been a case of a person which had in any which way been mistreated, injured, or anything of this kind had been reported by members of this family, if this had been documented, we would have taken these documents and then carried on our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: On that point -- I'm sorry, Mr. Stojkov, do you still have the Defence exhibit binder next to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I wonder if a copy could be made available for him. Or perhaps, actually, if we could just put it up on e-court, this might be easier. If we could put up Exhibit P00261.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen in front of you, Mr. Stojkov?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you remember telling Ms. Residovic that this is a document that you had seen and that you took a copy of this Official Note with you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if you look the subject, it says: "Report on a deceased person." In the first paragraph, the last line, it states: "An Official Note was taken during the interview, filed under number 535, on 13 August 2001, while the said person was able to communicate." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just to go back to the start of this paragraph, you will see that this relates to Atulla Qaili. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And it continues: "He was held at the Mirkovci police station from 0200 hours on 13 August 2001. On the same day, at about 0430 hours, as his health condition deteriorated, the duty officer at the Mirkovci police station called the ambulance and he was taken to the Skopje city hospital." "On 13 August 2001, the Skopje city hospital informed us that the aforementioned person had died during the day." Mr. Stojkov, wouldn't you consider this to be a report of an injured person at the police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What would you consider it to be?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information. It says up here "report." Where it is stated that the person Qaili Atulla, against whom a criminal report for the crime of terrorism was filed, it says that an official interview was conducted with him and that he was later taken to the city hospital where he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, weren't you at all curious about what led to this deterioration in his condition while he was at Mirkovci police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had not been curious, then I would not have known of this Official Note and the text therein. But I told you, after this report, the public prosecutor's office, it was the duty centre that informed the public prosecutor about this, and then this whole case was forwarded under the public prosecutor's hands. All measures taken further would have to be requested by the public prosecutor or investigating judge. As for me personally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In your mind, didn't this perhaps bring into question what you had been told informally by other police officers at the station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So you took no steps to find out what had happened to Atulla Qaili at the police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I say that any further engagement on my part as an authorised employee would have meant breach of legal regulations. I told you, once the case is taken over by the public prosecutor's office, we can work only upon their request.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know when the case was taken over by the public prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, after the report from the hospital to the police station that the person had died, the rule is that the duty centre must be immediately informed and the public prosecutor's office. So I think this was done on the same day or the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The same day or the following day. That would make it around about 13 or 14 August 2001. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is how it was done. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: But you didn't start your investigation, from my understanding, until approximately six months later?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Is that correct, sometime early in 2002, you commenced the investigation into Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember when we began the investigation. Certainly it was 2002, which means quite some time had elapsed since the death of this person. We did not have any information or requests from any service, neither from the public prosecutor, nor investigating judges, so that we could continue to show interest for the death of the person mentioned in this Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, the request for you to commence your investigation in early 2002, did that come from the public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding. The working group was working on cases or reports of injured parties. In this case we have a death of a person. It was immediately taken by the public prosecutor. If the public prosecutor had given us, as a working group, concrete tasks and charged us with carrying out certain investigations, we would have done so, because the public prosecutor, in this concrete case, did not have any requests nor any guidelines. We did not work on this case. We worked on the case file of Ljuboten as a whole, wanting to determine what had happened on that day, whether there are injured parties that reported any kind of injuries. I told you that we wanted to talk with certain persons from the village of Ljuboten, but that we were not successful in this. The case, the dossier, Ljuboten, if this is of interest to you, for me, is not a finished case, because I have not finished all things as -- as it should be. Unfortunately, though, the working group was disbanded. We did not get the official documents from the exhumation, from medical forensics. And after the working group was disbanded, we had the materials which we, until then, had been able to collect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, at the point that you were disbanded in 2003, would it be fair to say that the extent of your working group's investigation into the Ljuboten events consisted of collecting documents from OVR Cair and visits to Cair and Mirkovci police stations. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except our efforts to get in contact with persons, the data which we obtained from the Official Notes, our remaining tasks were to collect and gather information about the events that transpired at that time. We did not succeed in establishing contacts with persons to determine injured parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Would it also be fair to say that apart from the documents you collected, the already existing documents that you collected, all that you added to the case file was one Official Note about your visits to Cair and Mirkovci police stations?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was one note about the visits or if there was an Official Note about the activities we undertook or planned to undertake, but, in essence, it is how you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And beyond the documents you collected from OVR Cair, wouldn't you agree that the only other information that you've provided to this Tribunal comes from unrecorded, informal conversations you had with police officers in the stations?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our efforts to talk to persons from the village of Ljuboten, as I said, ended unsuccessfully because it was a post-conflict situation. Also, we had unsuccessful conversations with our colleagues, police officers, with whom we obtained information but we could not record them as official because they would not agree to having an official conversation with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So, overall, wouldn't you agree that this was a pretty unsuccessful investigation. It really didn't achieve much, did it?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for me, any investigation has the aim to clarify certain situation, and it's successful because efforts are made to try to clarify the situation. If you ask me about this particular case file and how it ended, I told you, personally, I'm not satisfied with the end because the group was disbanded. We were withdrawn from the working group and we were not able to finish what I wanted to finish, to have a complete case file after which activities could be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you were unable to speak to anyone who had actually been in the village on 12th August 2001, were you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In the course of your investigations, you did not manage to speak to a single person who had been inside Ljuboten on 13 August 2001, did you -- sorry, 12 August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated not during our work. I stated that from the moment when I myself opened the Ljuboten case file, and until the disbandment of the group or until before the exhumation, we did not succeed in establishing contacts with any of the persons mentioned or their relatives, those indicated in the official documents. And, at the same time, we did not find any documents where an aggrieved person or an injured party was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you were not able to obtain statements from any police officers either, were you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I already stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When the working group disbanded, do you know where its cases file relating to Ljuboten went?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment we were withdrawn from those tasks, there were still many materials remaining, not all of them were surrendered because there were closed case files and case files that were not closed. All documents were produced, as I said, in two copies and they were all organised in binders and they were transferred to the analytics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, is it the case that the working group was required to hand all the documentation relating to the Ljuboten investigation directly to the minister Ljube Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that all our documents related to the entire work of the group. After a certain number of interrelated case files or individual case files were completed, closed, we transferred them to the analytics department. Where they went from there onwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So if someone were to come before this Tribunal and say that your working group handed all its documentation directly to Minister Boskoski, they would be wrong?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they knew it was like that, I can't comment that. I know that we transferred, handed over the materials to the analytics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, I'm referring to the testimony of Sofija Galeva-Petrovska at page 8827.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab 21, please, Mr. Stojkov.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Stojkov and Your Honours, I'm going to skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, I'm going to put it to you now that isn't it true that your investigation simply consisted of collecting those documents that were already held by the Ministry of Interior at Cair police station?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to the Ljuboten case file, at that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And isn't it true that your working group made no real efforts to speak to any of the villagers from Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made efforts to establish contacts, but we did not succeed in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true that your working group conducted no interviews with either police or aggrieved persons from Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And isn't it true that the ultimate purpose of your working group was to collect information that corroborated what you had been told by police officers from police stations Cair and Mirkovci?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, I'll try to rephrase that. Isn't it true that the ultimate aim of what your working group was doing was simply to back up the story or the version of events you had been told by your fellow police officers?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn. I think this is a convenient time, then, for the second break, and we'll resume at half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Stojkov. Mr. Stojkov, do you remember having been asked by the Prosecutor when the work of your working group stopped, and your answer was that that was at the beginning of 2003. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure you'll also recall that your answer was that at the point in time when the work of your group ceased that there were quite a few cases that had not been completed. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, Mr. Stojkov, among those unfinished cases, was the Ljuboten case unfinished, the one that you worked on?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that one remained unfinished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, whether, among those unfinished cases, there were cases where the Macedonians were the injured party?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many such cases unfinished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when the work of your working group ceased, and that was at the beginning of 2003, do you remember who was the minister of the interior at that time?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a change in power. I believe that it was Mr. Hari Kostov, who was the minister. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boskoski, for several months, was not the minister at the time, nor was he in the ministry. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was not the minister any longer, so he was not with the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember, Mr. Stojkov, that my learned friend asked you on a number of occasions whether had you seen any reports from Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that he also asked you whether, in order to check out some information, you contacted and asked for assistance from Human Rights Watch. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that your answer was that at the time you didn't know that Human Rights Watch was conducting its own private investigation.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that I was not aware that some organisation or Human Rights Watch was conducting an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, even if you had had some information coming to you from the press or from NGOs or anything of that kind, tell me, would you have checked out that information too, in order to see whether the information was correct or not, true or not?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would not have verified them. We had an overview, as I stated, one that we received from the analytics services and that contained all information on persons and events.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness now be shown 65 ter 1D378.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, this is a letter addressed to the editor of the International Herald Tribune by the anti-defamation league or the league against defamation of character, libel. Now I'm going to read that text out to you: "[In English] Letters to the editor, in this rush to cast aspersions on Israel's actions in the conflict in Lebanon, Peter Bouckaert accuses Israel of indiscriminately attacking Lebanese civilians (for Israel, innocent civilians are fair game, August 4). Yet he is hardly an objective observer." "Bouckaert ignores the defensive context of Israel's military activity and is blind to the threat posed by Hezbollah. His skewed reporting for Human Rights Watch ignores the unprovoked attack that sparked the current conflict, along with Hezbollah's cynical strategy of using the Lebanese population as a human shield. Hezbollah fighters have been so successful in the current conflict by hiding among civilians." "There is great value in the work of objective witnesses in Lebanon. But Bouckaert's history of subjective and biased observation, especially when it comes to conflicts involving Israel, taints his analysis. Sincerely, Michael Salberg, Director, International Affairs." [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Stojkov, would it be fair to say that international organisations as well as individuals within them also had to have reliable --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It appears that this question is leading, Your Honour. I ask that it be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is re-examination, Ms. Residovic. If you could avoid leading, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Stojkov, what is your understanding of the work of international organisations? Tell me, having heard this article read out, to what extent do you consider that information of this kind must be checked out?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time, there were many non-governmental organisations in Macedonia and all media that existed in Macedonia at that time but also the international and foreign media, as far as I could see at that period, had different articles. But I think that anyone who wrote an article and signed it, should stand behind or should be guarantee for the veracity of it. I believe that the source should be protected but there should be evidence for what is written in the text. So I believe the same goes for this text.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Stojkov, do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you that if you were to read something in the papers in your country, that would you check that out?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember and I stated if there had been an event, that would cause our services that means the police, the Ministry of Interior, public prosecutor's office, if they had any reason to suspect that a crime had been committed, then they would verify the accuracy of the allegation. If there were any suspicions that a crime has been committed, then I am sure the services would have taken some action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So as a policemen, tell me whether you must first establish that an act had been committed in the first place for you to be able to continue?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person reports -- if a person comes to a police station and reports that any crime had been committed, then a minute is taken in order to prepare a criminal report and then those allegations are entered as data in the criminal report. If there is no complaint, then we cannot operate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But as the Prosecutor suggested and put to you, if you just had some news in the media about something, for a policeman would that be enough? Would it be sufficient for him to say that the event was true and correct and that there were grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, Mr. Stojkov, that the Prosecutor also asked you the following: He asked you whether you had contacted the OSCE in Macedonia to help you to conduct an investigation into the case and that you said that you didn't have the power to do that, that it wasn't within your competence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you also remember that the Prosecutor asked you whether you had contacted any Albanian politicians, for example, and that your answer was that that wasn't within your powers and that, therefore, you did not do so. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, if a general of the police, for example, who was the under-secretary in the ministry for the uniformed police, and if he were to contact the OSCE or EU or NATO or the Albanian politicians or anything like that, then would that be an individual who would be in a position to contact them and not just an inspector like you? Would they be best placed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from my position based on the competences entrusted to us then, but also now, I should not be able to establish such contacts. A person should be authorised to have such contacts. What would that person's rank be and position within the ministry, I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But what I'm asking is this. If somebody at that position did that -- did that, would that be all right, or don't you have a position in the matter?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the needs or the interests of the ministry so require or the needs or the interest of the state, the Republic of Macedonia, I wouldn't have anything against that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to draw your attention to the testimony of General Risto Galevski on page 3770 to 71 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that yesterday the Prosecutor asked you about your professional experience and the way in which you performed your duties and that you gave him precise answers to those questions and said that you were commended a number of times for your work. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, in view of this professional experience of yours and the way in which you worked, did your -- were your superiors able to rely on you and the work did you, the work you were assigned to do?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure they relied on my personal work and the work of the group because we were appointed. And knowing our prior background, I believe they had faith in us and they relied on what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Prosecutor also asked you yesterday something about what your understanding on -- was of the Law on Amnesty, governing amnesty and you said that you weren't a lawyer but that you knew that the Law on Amnesty was enacted. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you know that certain acts were exempt from amnesty and what organs are there to assess as to whether an act or event can be amnestied or not comes under the Law of Amnesty or not?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say with certainty that I was aware that some events were exempt from amnesty, but that assessment was made by the public prosecutor's office and the court in the Republic of Macedonia or at least I think so, I'm not sure. I believe that they should be the ones to assess whether there is a possibility for a deed to be exempt from that or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, would you look at your binder, the one that the Prosecutor gave you, and take a look at a document after page 21 -- or partition 21. And it is 65 ter 1D594, after tab 21. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you can also find it after tab 21. You have the English version first, followed by the text in Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that the sector for analytics and research sent the crime department of the police, through Mr. Sofevski, a request to provide a report. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Spasen Sofevski was in fact the under-secretary in charge of the crime police, and he was at the top of the chain of command, was he not?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And as you said that at the beginning of 2002 sometime, you were given the assignment of opening up the case of Ljuboten, but that you didn't know what period of time this was precisely, you couldn't be more precise. You said it might have been February or March, but at all events it was at the beginning of 2002. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to take a look at paragraph 1 where it says that: "The Ministry of Justice, with written communication of the 14th of February 2002, to the minister of the interior, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, requested from this ministry the dispatch as soon as possible of information requested in Prosecutor Mr. Andrew Cayley's letter of the 30th of January, 2002, to the government of the Republic of Macedonia." Mr. Stojkov, in view of this first paragraph, could -- or, rather, how do you understand this paragraph? What would your conclusions be? Is it the minister who received this request, was he the individual who in fact sent on the request to the competent authorities, his superiors? Would that be your understanding?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter -- or, rather, a request to provide certain reports and documents sent by the Ministry of Justice and then through analytics sector through the then under-secretary should be forwarded to the minister at the time, Mr. Ljube Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph at the end of that paragraph you can see that this request was linked to two events, Neprosteno and Ljuboten. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in the last paragraph it says: "We kindly ask you to dispatch the following to this sector as soon as possible in order that we may respond to the aforementioned requests." "Copies of police dossiers, if they are complete, on the investigation undertaken into the events in the village of Neprosteno; and if they are not complete, then a detailed report on the current situation with regard to the investigation, including copies of witness statements, if they exist." "Report on the current situation with regard to the police investigation into the events in the village of Ljuboten (if there is such an investigation), including witness statements, if there are such statements." "Copies of any other official reports or other documentation which relate to the events in the villages of Neprosteno and Ljuboten, or refer to the aforementioned investigation." Mr. Stojkov, would you agree with me that this document speaks about the need to gather certain documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Actually, sorry, I'll withdraw that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, in answering the questions put to you, do you remember having said that your working group did not have the task of replacing the competent organs. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you also remember that when the Prosecutor asked you, you repeated the method of work you applied, and you repeated that several times.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not up to us to replace the police stations and the OVRs that were active at a given territory. Our work and our gathering of evidence had its own purposes and aims, but I believe that if we arrived at some data and if we arrived at witnesses or witness statements or any other document based on which we would have grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed, then we would have informed the sector and the department for analytics that then forward the documents to the OVRs, departments of internal affairs that prepare the documents and then forward them to the basic public prosecutor's office and then they prepare an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember, Mr. Stojkov, that today the Prosecutor repeated the example that you gave from the village of Aracinovo, when you showed that for certain theft that had taken place, significant theft of Albanian property, Macedonian policemen were reported. Do you remember the Prosecutor asking you that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members from the reserve police forces, not active police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the Prosecutor asked you whether this sort of theft would be considered a war crime. Do you remember him asking you that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, do you know that a legal evaluation and assessment of an event -- well, let me put it this way. Do you know who makes the legal assessment, whether it is the police, the prosecutor, the Court? Who is it that does that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police can give the grounds or to interpret a criminal act. However, it is the prosecutor, in preparing the indictment, who provides the law, or rather, the article of the Macedonian law pursuant to which the crime will be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness now be shown the following document, please, P81. And that is the Criminal Law of the Republic of Macedonia, Article 404. The Macedonian version is ERN number 26927, the Macedonian version, and the English version is ERN 005544. And as I said, it's Article 404.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you recognise the title page of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in Article 404, we have a series of crimes against the civilian population listed. And in the first part, paragraph 1, it is an instance in war, during a war, armed conflict or occupation. Do you agree with me that that's what it says at the beginning of paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at line 7 from the bottom of that paragraph. I'm going to read it out. I'm going to read out what acts could be considered war crimes against the civilian population. It is looting, pilfering of property of the population, illegal and [indiscernible] destruction, or usurpation of a large extent of properties which is not justified by military needs. Now, tell me, Mr. Stojkov, do you agree with me when I say that within the frameworks of that Article we have different types of theft and looting, which is incorporated into this paragraph 1 of the Article?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And whether something is considered theft or not, it is the organs of law and authority that are going to decide about it, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is true. It is the courts that decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you -- or, rather, let me put it this way. You said that you would always go to the police station or internal affairs organ where the act has been reported to take some documents from them which would help you in your work, which would be important to you in your work. Right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask to you take a look at the next document after tab 5, which is P565. The document is under seal. And on page N006-7661, ERN number. That's the English version. N006-7652, N006-7673. It's page 7 of eleven pages. Yes, the English is fine then. And we need the Macedonian version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, you saw this document when it was put to you by the Prosecutor, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And at the top of the document it says that it's an organ of the Ministry of Interior in Tetovo, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is a record compiled by some authorised person when the injured party himself personally came to report the incident, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And at the end of this record, attached to it is the documentation that the injured party brought to back up his claims, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 006-765661, ERN number, that is. No, I apologise. N006-7658; that's the Macedonian version. And the English version is number N006-7658. And you have also seen this document, have you not? It is also, I'm sure you'll agree with me, that it was also taken over by the organs of the interior in Tetovo. This is to say, the authority in Tetovo, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Much earlier on, before the injured party, that is to say at the time when this happened, and that was the 6th of July, 2001. Is that what it says in this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says the 6th and the 7th of July, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood your explanations, how you explained it to me, and how you explained it to the Prosecutor, when he put a number of questions to you about this, your method of work was the following: You went to the police station, and then you would take the documents that you would find there, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And at the police station, in this particular police station, you found this report and some of the activities that the police station undertook within its remitt and authority, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you also went on to explain your method of work, and said that you tried on that occasion to talk to the injured party or members of his family, and once you managed to do that on a voluntary basis, you talked to them, interviewed them and compiled an official report, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was our way of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please, I'm going to ask you how you worked in Ljuboten. When the Prosecutor asked you, you said that you went to the police station Mirkovci and then to the one in Cair, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, is there any difference in that and in what you did when you went to the Tetovo organ of the Ministry of the Interior in the previous case?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no difference. This is our principle of work. We always began with the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the police station in Cair, you asked to see the documents, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We requested documents about the event in the village of Ljuboten with the dates I mentioned previously, somewhat before and somewhat after the event itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any difference in your method of work there and in the previous case and when you went to Tetovo looking for documents which the police station had in its possession?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The manner is identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering the questions put to you, you said that you managed to gain information about certain individuals whom could have been injured parties themselves and that, first, from your colleagues and then through your own personal efforts, you tried to reach those injured parties themselves. Do you remember saying that and telling the Prosecutor that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is part of the procedure which we followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So is that any different than the way you went about this in Tetovo when you learnt about the event described in this document or dossier 565, file 565? Did you try to reach the injured party there too?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct, the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the only difference being -- or, rather, did you find the injured party there and did you find the injured party in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ljuboten, as I said, we were not able to establish contact with a person who would come forth as injured parties or their close relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the next document, which comes after tab 11. And to refresh your memory that was one of the documents that the Prosecutor showed you as well, right? It is Exhibit P569 and the first page in English is N006-781. And it says that it is photo documentation and then we have page N006-7881. That's the first page of this document in Macedonian. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, you covered a number of -- you looked at a number of photographs from this photo documentation set with the Prosecutor, they were shown to you.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you observed that the individual who was shown here as being the individuals providing information -- the individual providing information was in fact an Albanian, right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an inspector with many years of experience, and as a member of the working group as well, can you tell me whether it is important to conduct an on-site investigation and gather photo documentation about the event, about the event that -- or incident that took place?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important immediately after any kind of crime to have on-site investigation. Records are made of this on-site investigation, evidence is marked, photo documentation is prepared. This is one of the basic rules of investigation. The basic rules that allow the investigations to go on. Without an on-site investigation, we cannot document the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that this on-site investigation and the photo documentation and the other documents contained in this file was compiled by the competent authority within the Ministry of the Interior who, by law, is duty-bound to act in this way and uncover the -- uncover crimes and the perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, as in the other cases, the police station or the OVR, the territory in which the crime had happened, is in charge for undertaking all measures to investigate or to proceed with measure prescribed by law to elucidate this crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you've already explained this to us, is my understanding of the matter correct, that you were not able to replace the work of those organs, nor was it your task for you to be the investigators of all these events?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not have replaced the work of the police station or the OVR in any case. These are tasks, works regulated by law that have to be carried out by the police station or the OVR.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if this case shown to you by the Prosecutor, if I were to compare that or if we were to compare that with your efforts to learn something about what had happened in and around Ljuboten, then, tell me this: Did you have an opportunity in the documents from the Mirkovci police station or the Cair police station to find material related to the on-site investigation along with all the photo documentation and everything necessary for a case to be documented or an incident which had happened to be documented?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not find anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find any documents at all which would show whether any attempts had been made to enter the village, for instance?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what the chief Krstevski at the time told me in our discussions also. Later I found it in an information or Official Note, I can't recall now, where it is listed that on two occasions on-site investigations teams were formed with medical teams, with certainly a public prosecutor or a judge or other colleagues from the MOI to carry on an on-site investigation in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we were to compare this to the previous instance, the fact that there was no investigation -- or, rather, on-site investigation, to what extent could this influence help you throw light on the case? How would that help you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, there was no reported case. And, secondly, if an on-site investigation had been carried out, if the on-site investigation teams of SVR Skopje, inspectors from OVR Cair and the other responsible bodies had gone to the site and if had been documented as the other example, then, the possibilities would be much better to complete and to bring all things to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your answer to a question from the Prosecutor, Mr. Stojkov, when you said that you hoped that the results of the exhumation and post-mortem could provide you with new information to enable you to continue with your work and investigation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because as I said there was no on-site investigation immediately after the events in Ljuboten. We expected, first of all, that we, too, as a working group would be present at the exhumation but we were not allowed to do so. Later, we expected the results of the exhumation and the results of forensic medicine. This would have meant some official which would allow us to undertake further measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question to you is this: As an inspector with a lot of experience, can you tell me, to what extent an autopsy can help the police in establishing the cause of death, the way in which death occurred and to clear up the question of whether it was a killing, a suicide or how a death occurred. Can an autopsy help an inspector to arrive at any conclusions in that respect?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, for a period of time, I worked as an assistant to my colleague at the homicide unit. But having seen how things are -- and work is conducted there that the autopsy and the reports of forensic medicine which provide these autopsies are very useful to throwing light on a crime where death has occurred, regardless of how this death has occurred. As we know the time of death is given, the cause of death, the manner in which the death occurred, and I believe this is very useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojkov, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. Mr. Stojkov, you will be pleased to know that concludes the questioning of you. The Chamber would thank you for your assistance and for your attendance here in The Hague and you are now, of course, free to return to your home and your ordinary activities. And the court officer will show you out. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for this possibility to be here at the Tribunal and to share my experiences of this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Earlier this afternoon the Chamber received information that the intended next witness was in considerable pain despite medical attention and needed to go to his bed and rest so that we have no prospect of continuing now. In any event, our time effectively has been almost completely exhausted. The experience of the last couple of days suggest to us that it may be better, in view of the reported problems with the next witness's back, if we sit for only two sessions, each of about an hour and a half, tomorrow and Friday in the hope that this will enable the witness to be with us at least for three effective hours of evidence during the day. It's possible that that may prove too much, but we will attempt that. If there's no other matter -- oh, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, have I received strict instructions from my case manager and from the registry officer to place the following information on the record, that we will be replacing a draft English translation of Exhibit P00063 with a final translation, and we will be linking an additional translation to Exhibit P00533. I have just been asked to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. We will adjourn now and we resume at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of February, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
